subsection: 5. Fabric construction, finishes, colour, design and testing

notes.b: Woven fabric is made by interlacing two sets of yarns at right angles on a loom (the frame that holds the yarns). The way the yarns cross each other decides how firm, smooth or hard wearing the fabric is.
points: Warp yarns run lengthways and are held under tension on the loom; weft yarns are passed across them at right angles, over and under the warp.
Plain weave: each weft yarn passes alternately over and under each warp yarn. It is the simplest and most stable interlacing, so it is firm and hard wearing, as in calico and cotton shirting.

Twill weave: each weft passes over two or more warp yarns before passing under one, and the pattern shifts each row, forming diagonal lines. Twill is more drapable and hard wearing than plain weave, as in denim.

Satin weave: long floats (stretches of yarn lying loose on the surface) cross with few interlacings, giving a smooth, lustrous face. Because the floats are long, satin is less durable and more prone to snagging.
Plain, twill and satin are the three basic weaves.
Selvedges: the tightly woven edges formed where the weft turns back. They resist fraying, so the edges of the fabric do not unravel.
Diagram: interlacing grids for plain, twill and satin weaves, marking the warp and weft yarns that pass over or under at each crossing.
notes.tip: When asked to describe a construction technique for a named fibre, name the weave and explain warp, weft and selvedge. Examiners ask for all three terms.

notes.b: Knitted fabric is formed from a series of interlocking loops of yarn, made by hand with needles or by machine. Loops can open and close, so the fabric stretches and recovers its shape.
points: Weft knitting: loops are formed across each row, so usually one yarn can make the whole fabric. Warp knitting is machine-made, with the yarn zigzagging along the length of the fabric.
Plain (jersey) knit: loops are formed in one direction on each row, giving a smooth face and a looped reverse. It stretches across the width and is used for T-shirts.
Rib knit: knit and purl columns alternate, typically 1 by 1, giving elasticity in both directions, so it suits cuffs and waistbands.
Purl knit: loops are pulled to the reverse side, producing the purl face of a fabric, the reverse of a plain knit. Purl is a looping method, not a different kind of fabric.
Double knit: two sets of needles make a double-thickness fabric that is warm and reversible.
Knitted fabric is stretchy and flexible, with the amount of stretch depending on the yarn used and the looping structure. It is also comfortable and drapes well.
Knitted fabric is warm because its loops trap air, and it can be knitted into shaped pieces or garments with few seams, or none. It may snag, sag or shrink.
Uses include jumpers, hats, scarves, socks, T-shirts, blankets and throws.
notes.tip: Knitting is a 9-mark explanation at Higher Level (2019H, 2005H). Cover loops, weft against warp knitting, plain, rib and purl, then properties and uses.

notes.h: Felting, non-woven bonding and other constructions (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Fabric does not always need yarn. Fibres can be locked together directly, which gives a third construction technique beyond weaving and knitting.
points: Felting: wool fibres are matted together by heat, moisture and agitation (pressure). The scales on each fibre interlock, so no yarn is needed.
Non-woven bonding: fibres are fixed into a web using adhesive, heat or needle punching, forming a fabric without weaving or knitting.
Needle punching: barbed needles push fibres through a web, interlocking them mechanically.
Felt is used for hats, interlinings and insulation; bonded non-woven fabrics are used for interlinings and disposable items.
Crochet, lace and macramé are other constructions that appear in marking schemes.
notes.tip: Marking schemes accept bonding as a construction technique, so you can name it as your third technique.

notes.b: A finish is applied after weaving or knitting to change the fabric's appearance, handle (how it feels) or performance. Finishes are used to prevent creasing and shrinkage, add water repellence or stain resistance, increase durability and safety, improve wear and prevent loss of colour.
points: Crease-resistant finish: a resin cross-links the cellulose in cotton and linen so the fabric resists wrinkling, which means less ironing, for example on a linen skirt. It can slightly reduce strength and absorbency.
Water-repellent finish: a silicone coating makes water bead on the surface and run off, as on raincoats and tablecloths.
Stain-resistant finish: spills sit on the surface so they can be wiped away before they soak in, as on jackets, upholstery and tablecloths.
Anti-static finish: applied to synthetic fibres, or added at home through a fabric conditioner, to reduce static build-up and cling, for example in dresses and linings.
Flame-retardant finish: reduces how easily the fabric burns, so it is used on household textiles and nightwear.
Mercerising: cotton is treated with caustic soda, which makes it stronger, lustrous and more absorbent, as in bed sheets and jeans.
notes.tip: For a six-mark question on why finishes are used, give three reasons with a point of explanation each. When asked to name one finish, give its purpose and an example of use, such as waterproofing for a raincoat. Waterproof (coated, blocks water) and water repellent (water beads and runs off) are different, but examiners accept the word waterproofing for either. A finish goes on after the fabric is made.

notes.h: Calendering and shrink resistance (Higher Level only)
notes.b: At Higher Level you must know a third finish. Either of these two will do.
points: Calendering: fabric is passed between heated rollers under pressure, flattening the surface to give a smooth, glossy or embossed finish.
Shrink resistance: a finish or controlled pre-treatment reduces the shrinkage of cotton and wool during washing, so the garment keeps its size.

notes.b: Colour is applied either by dyeing or by printing a design onto the surface. Dyeing colours the fibre, yarn or fabric, and the dye must be matched to the fibre type.
points: Reactive dyes form strong chemical bonds with cotton and linen, giving bright, washfast colour. Cotton takes reactive dyes, not acid or disperse dyes.
Acid dyes are used on protein fibres such as wool and silk, and on nylon, in an acidic dye bath.
Disperse dyes are used on polyester and acetate, applied as fine particles dispersed in water.
Yarn dyeing: yarn is dyed before weaving or knitting, so it produces stripes, checks and tweeds.
Piece dyeing: the finished fabric is dyed in one plain colour after it has been constructed.
notes.tip: When asked for a colour method suitable for a named fibre, match the dye to it: reactive for cotton, acid for wool, silk and nylon, disperse for polyester and acetate. Yarn dyeing is done before weaving or knitting.

notes.h: Colour application: printing and resist methods
notes.b: Printing places colour on the surface of a made fabric in a pattern, while resist methods block dye from parts of the fabric so those parts stay undyed.
points: Screen printing: a stencil on a fine mesh screen blocks off the areas that should not print, and ink is pushed through the open mesh with a squeegee. Each colour needs its own screen.
Roller printing: engraved rollers, one for each colour, print the fabric continuously and quickly, so it suits long runs.
Stencilling: a cut stencil and sponge are used, which is simple and suits children's clothing.
Transfer printing: the design is printed on paper, and heat transfers it to polyester.
Resist dyeing: wax (batik) or tying (tie-dye) stops dye reaching parts of the fabric, leaving a pattern.
Diagram: cross-section of a screen-printing stage showing the screen, stencil, squeegee, ink and the fabric beneath on a padded table.
notes.tip: Printing and tie-dye appear under both colour application and design application in schemes. If a question asks for both, give a different method for each part.

notes.b: Design is applied to a fabric by adding decoration once the fabric has been made. Each technique gives a different look and suits different garments.
points: Appliqué: a shaped piece of fabric is attached to a background with stitching, with raw edges turned under or satin stitched, as for logos and jackets.
Embroidery: decorative threads are stitched onto the fabric surface by hand or machine, for example cross stitch or chain stitch.
Quilting: a top fabric, wadding and backing are stitched together through all layers, trapping the wadding in a pattern.
Patchwork: pieces of fabric are sewn together to form a design, often combined with quilting.
Smocking: fabric is gathered and held in pleats by stitching in a pattern, giving stretch and decoration, often on children's clothing.
Embossing: a heated, patterned roller presses a raised design into the fabric surface.
Beading and sequins: small pieces are sewn on by hand or machine to add sparkle and texture.
Printing (screen, roller, stencil, transfer) also counts as design application in marking schemes.
notes.tip: Choose a method that suits the fabric or garment in the question, such as smocking or stencilling for children's clothing, and describe how it is done.

notes.b: Performance tests compare fabrics under identical conditions to judge their suitability for a particular use, such as a school jacket or uniform.
points: Fair test: samples are cut to the same size with the grain in the same direction, conditioned in the same room, and tested under the same load and time. This way only the fabric differs.

Crease-recovery test: a sample is folded in half, placed under a set weight for a set time, then released and left to recover. The angle between the two halves is measured with a protractor, and the angle closest to 180 degrees shows the best recovery.
Another crease method is to crumple equal samples in a closed fist for one minute, release them and compare on a five-point scale.
Absorbency test: a set volume of water is dropped onto the fabric and the time it takes to soak in is recorded. A fabric that absorbs quickly is suited to towels.

Colourfastness test: a sample is sewn between white fabrics and washed in a detergent solution. The change in colour of the sample and the staining of the white fabrics are compared with a grey scale.
Shrinkage test: a sample is measured, washed at a set temperature, dried and measured again, and the percentage change is calculated.
Repeat each test and calculate an average so that a single result does not mislead.
Other tests named in schemes: abrasion, insulation, stretch, pilling or snagging, tearing, water resistance and flame resistance.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name one or two tests and give the procedure for one. Write the fair-test conditions, how you measure, and the conclusion you draw from the result.

keyTerms.definition: The lengthwise yarns held under tension on a loom, across which the weft is woven.
The yarns passed across the warp at right angles during weaving.
The tightly woven edge of a woven fabric, formed where the weft turns back, which resists fraying.
A weave in which the weft passes over two or more warp yarns before passing under one, forming diagonal lines.
A method of knitting in which loops are formed across each row from a single yarn.
The matting of wool fibres together by heat, moisture and agitation so that their scales interlock.
A treatment applied to a fabric to improve its performance, such as crease resistance, water repellence or stain resistance.
A dye that forms strong chemical bonds with cellulose fibres such as cotton and linen.
A printing method in which ink is pushed through a stencilled mesh screen onto the fabric, with one screen for each colour.
A design method in which a shaped piece of fabric is attached to a background by stitching.
A performance test that measures how far a folded fabric opens after a set load is removed.

questions.prompt: Name two fabric construction techniques and describe how one of them forms a fabric.
questions.model: Weaving and knitting. Weaving: warp yarns are held under tension on a loom and weft yarns pass across them at right angles, with each weft passing over and under the warp in a set pattern to interlace the two sets of yarns. Knitting: loops of yarn are pulled through previous loops to form a fabric; loops formed across each row give weft knitting, which stretches and recovers its shape.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the construction, finish, colour application, design application and performance testing of a fabric affect its suitability for its end use. Refer to at least one functional finish, one colour application method, one design application method and one performance test.
questions.model: Construction: a plain or twill weave gives a stable, durable fabric suited to shirts or workwear, while a knitted fabric stretches and recovers its shape, suiting T-shirts and sportswear. Finish: a crease-resistant resin finish on cotton reduces wrinkling and suits a shirt that must look neat after washing, though it may slightly reduce strength. Colour: screen printing, with one screen per colour, gives a clear, repeatable pattern on a cotton fabric, while reactive dyes give bright, washfast colour. Design: appliqué or embroidery adds decoration to a fabric without weakening it and suits a child's garment. Performance testing: a crease-recovery test, carried out under identical conditions, measures how far a folded sample opens, so that a shirt fabric can be chosen with the best recovery; an absorbency test shows whether a fabric suits towels.
